newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-Shell refining output cuts signal tough times.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shell refining output cuts signal tough times.

text.p: Shell Singapore's decision to cut products output by a hefty 15 percent signalled tough times ahead for the industry as it grapples with new capacity and exports from the West, industry sources said on Wednesday.

Shell Singapore, a unit of Royal Dutch Shell, announced a 9,000-tonne-per-day (TPD) cut in output from June 27 at its refinery on the southern island of Pulau Bukom which has a 59,000-TPD (435,000 barrels per day) capacity.
"That is a huge cut, but for margins to improve the fundamentals need to change," a trader at a major oil company said. "We need China to come out and buy in a big way."
Another trader said that other refiners, including those outside Singapore, also need to cut production in order to lift the market.

Shell, Singapore's largest refiner said the cuts will be maintained until market conditions improve. The company has also scheduled a one-week shutdown of a 115,000-bpd crude unit for maintenance from July 6.
Industry sources said another refiner, Esso Singapore has cut output by 10 percent late last week at its 230,000-bpd refinery. But an Esso spokeswoman declined to comment.
But two other refiners, Mobil Oil Singapore and Singapore Refining Co (SRC) are not likely to join the cut in output due to different internal needs.
Mobil is maintaining output at its 300,000-bpd refinery as it builds up feedstocks for a new lubricant base oil plant due to start production in the third quarter, a company source said.
SRC is not cutting back despite high stocks at its 280,000-bpd refinery because of the different needs of its three share holders, a source close to the refiner said.
SRC is a joint-venture between British Petroleum, Singapore Petroleum Corp and Caltex, itself a joint venture between Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp.
Industry sources said Shell and Esso were forced to cut production due to high stocks of diesel and fuel oil in the face of poor regional demand.
Singapore refineries are the region's swing producer and a key refining barometer despite making up only 1.3 million bpd of Asia's total 18.1 million bpd capacity.
Refining sources said basic oil processing returns are almost in the red with most not making any profits for every barrel refined at the basic stage.
The refiners' predicament are both seasonal as well structural due in part to the 1.2-million bpd increase in refining capacity in 1996, with South Korea adding 620,000-bpd.
The step increase in refining capacity has led to oversupply whenever there is a lull in demand, traders said.
"Currently the Koreans, Japanese and even Thais are offering gas oil for export," one trader said. Gas oil or diesel makes up about 60 percent of a refinery's output after reprocessing.
The supply overhang was aggravated by record exports of more than three million tonnes of diesel over a two-month period from the West to Asia, arriving since late May.

Traders said the large exports from the West are becoming a feature of Asia's new trading pattern because spot prices could be bid up sharply and make it economical to bring cargoes from other regions to Asia.

"People just lock in the high prices in the swaps market and bring the cargoes here," one trader said. "But not all of them find a home for these cargoes and a lot of the cargoes are sold at the expense of the local refiners."
As a result, storage tanks in Singapore are brimming because of the limited demand.
"The only way to get rid of these supplies is if China buys and China has yet to signal its intention," another trader said.
Refiners said they are weary of their over-reliance on China to shore up profits due to the unpredicatable buying pattern of the Asian giant and are seeking other markets.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3093)
